title: Loop Engineering
summary: Loop Engineering is the design of a repeatable agentic control cycle that lets an AI agent continue working toward a goal across multiple turns. A production loop combines instructions and context with tool use, feedback or verification, state updates, retry policy, resource limits, human checkpoints, and explicit completion or escalation conditions.
definition: Loop Engineering is the design of a repeatable agentic control cycle that lets an AI agent continue working toward a goal across multiple turns. A production loop combines instructions and context with tool use, feedback or verification, state updates, retry policy, resource limits, human checkpoints, and explicit completion or escalation conditions. Mature loop design also accounts for resumability and observability so long-running work can pause, recover, and be inspected rather than behaving as an opaque sequence of repeated prompts.

audiences.seniorLeaders: Loop Engineering converts autonomy into an operational control problem. Leaders must decide what the agent may do repeatedly, which actions require approval, what counts as success, how much time or money a run may consume, what evidence a verifier must check, and when the agent must stop or escalate. Production agent runtimes now implement loops, guardrails, sessions, human-in-the-loop controls, and tracing as first-class capabilities, making these decisions directly relevant to deployment governance.
audiences.knowledgeWorkers: Knowledge workers increasingly define the objective and acceptance criteria, then supervise exceptions rather than directing every intermediate action. The critical skill is designing a trustworthy feedback signal: a loop that optimizes against a weak verifier can become faster at producing the wrong result.

example: A research agent retrieves approved sources, drafts findings, runs a claim-support check, and retries unsupported claims with targeted retrieval. It checkpoints its state before consequential steps, pauses for human review when evidence remains ambiguous, and terminates when coverage, source-quality, and budget criteria are satisfied.
opportunities: and measurable optimization of cost per successful task rather than cost per model response
risks: and failure to escalate when progress stalls

A correct final answer can still conceal an unsafe, wasteful, or unstable trajectory.
monitor: Successful-task rate; verifier precision and false approvals; average iterations; no-progress detection; guardrail trips; human-interrupt rate; checkpoint and resume success; cost per successful run; tool-path stability; trace-level evaluation; and whether increasing autonomy improves outcomes without weakening control.
